title: Scaling Laws for Classical Machine Learning on Tabular Data: A Benchmark Study
abstract: Prior classical-ML learning-curve work fits power laws to tree, linear, and kernel models on tabular data, but at small scale: typically one curve, one team, a handful of cells. We present a distributed classroom-scale replication: 127 students each ran a fixed protocol on 3 assigned datasets, drawn from 18 tabular classification and regression datasets and 6 model families (Boosting, Random Forest, SVM, Linear/Logistic, Ridge, Lasso), yielding 11,536 training runs and 1,648 fitted power-law curves of the form error(N) = a N^(-b) + c. Three findings. (1) Power laws fit: R^2 > 0.8 on 77.7% of cells, with tree ensembles dominating at full data (Boosting 50% of datasets, RandomForest 33%; linear models underperform on classification). (2) Approximate shared exponents within a model family: for 5 of 6 families, a single family-level exponent predicts each family's cross-dataset curves nearly as well as per-dataset exponents (R^2 gap < 0.011), though AIC favors the unconstrained fit and curve collapse is partial (32-58% of points within +/-0.5 dex). We frame this as approximate predictive compressibility, not dataset-independent universality; Lasso fails outright (negative control) and Ridge is fragile under leave-one-dataset-out. (3) Replicator-implementation variance: with random_state=42 fixed, independent re-implementations of the same protocol still differ by mean CV(b) = 0.144 on the fitted exponent -- not seed variance, but the spread induced by unconstrained parts of the protocol (preprocessing, encoding, missing-value handling). We release the aggregated curves, per-cell fits, and a practical data-requirement table for N* to reach target error 0.15.

(1) Power laws fit: R 2 > 0.8 R^{2}>0.8 on 77.7% of cells, with tree ensembles dominating at full data (Boosting 50% of datasets, RandomForest 33%; linear models underperform on classification). (2) Approximate shared exponents within a model family: for 5 of 6 families, a single family-level exponent predicts each family’s cross-dataset curves nearly as well as per-dataset exponents ( R 2 R^{2} gap < 0.011 <0.011 ), though AIC favors the unconstrained fit and curve collapse is partial (32–58% of points within ± 0.5 \pm 0.5 dex). (3) Replicator-implementation variance: with random_state=42 fixed, independent re-implementations of the same protocol still differ by mean CV ​ ( b ) = 0.144 \mathrm{CV}(b)=0.144 on the fitted exponent—not seed variance, but the spread induced by unconstrained parts of the protocol (preprocessing, encoding, missing-value handling). We release the aggregated curves, per-cell fits, and a practical data-requirement table for N ⋆ N^{\star} to reach target error 0.15 0.15 . 1 Introduction Empirical scaling laws have become central to how large neural networks are designed, trained, and budgeted: predictable power-law decay of test loss with model size, dataset size, and compute now informs decisions worth tens of millions of dollars per training run (Kaplan et al. , 2020 ; Hoffmann et al. , 2022 ; Hestness et al. , 2017 ; Rosenfeld et al. , 2020 ) . Yet the overwhelming majority of applied machine learning in industry is not large neural networks on text or images. It is gradient-boosted trees, random forests, and linear models on tabular business data—churn prediction, default risk, sales forecasting, ad-click prediction, and causal market segmentation (Ding et al. , 2024 ) . These are precisely the settings where tree ensembles continue to outperform deep learning (Grinsztajn et al. , 2022 ; Shwartz-Ziv and Armon, 2022 ) . While a classical-ML learning-curve literature exists (Perlich et al. , 2003 ; Mukherjee et al. , 2003 ; Figueroa et al. , 2012 ; Domhan et al. , 2015 ) , no prior study to our knowledge characterizes how their generalization error scales with training-set size at the cross-replicator scale that Kaplan et al. achieved for transformers within a single research team. Our contribution is not the idea of fitting a power law to a tree- or linear-model learning curve but scale of replication : we run a single fixed protocol 127 times, once per student in a graduate ML course (each student randomly assigned 3 of 18 datasets), yielding 11,536 model fits and 1,648 successful scaling curves. This lets us measure both the exponents and their variance across nominally compliant re-implementations. Our contributions are: • Approximate shared exponents within a model family : We separate three levels of claim. (a) Fit : the additive power law describes individual curves well (77.7% with R 2 > 0.8 R^{2}>0.8 ). (b) Compression : a single family-level b m b_{m} replaces per-dataset b m , d b_{m,d} with small predictive loss ( R 2 R^{2} gap < 0.011 <0.011 on 5 of 6 families; held-out LODO gap ≤ 0.012 \leq 0.012 for Boosting, RandomForest, LinearModel). (c) Universality ( b m , d = b m b_{m,d}=b_{m} ): not supported —AIC favors per-dataset fits, curve collapse is partial, and a permutation null shows the in-sample gap lacks specificity. Lasso fails outright as a negative control; Ridge is fragile (LODO CV 0.96 0.96 ). The contribution is the compression result, not universality. • Empirical benchmark : 18 datasets × \times 6 model families × \times 7 nested training fractions, 11,536 runs aggregated from 127 students; tree ensembles win at full data (Boosting 50%, RandomForest 33%). • Replicator-implementation variance : With random_state=42 fixed, CV ​ ( b ) = 0.144 \mathrm{CV}(b)=0.144 across students measures unconstrained-protocol spread (preprocessing, encoding, missing-value handling), not seed variance. • Practical data-requirement curves : pooled-fit N ⋆ N^{\star} to reach 0.15 0.15 target error, with cells where the floor c ≥ 0.15 c\geq 0.15 flagged as unreachable for that model. 2 Related Work Neural scaling laws. A line of work beginning with Hestness et al. ( 2017 ) and crystallized by Kaplan et al. ( 2020 ) established that neural language-model test loss follows a clean power law in model size, dataset size, and compute. The Chinchilla paper (Hoffmann et al. , 2022 ) refined the joint parameter–data tradeoff and showed that prior large models were systematically undertrained. Rosenfeld et al. ( 2020 ) extended the formalism to image classification and proposed the additive-irreducible-error parameterization a ​ N − b + c aN^{-b}+c that we adopt directly. These results are all on neural models—transformers, ResNets, recurrent nets—and at moderately large data scales. Whether the same functional form applies to gradient-boosted trees on a few thousand tabular rows has, until now, not been settled empirically at scale. Classical-ML learning curves. Fitting power laws to classical-ML learning curves is itself a long-studied topic that predates the neural-scaling-laws literature. Perlich et al. ( 2003 ) fit learning curves for tree induction versus logistic regression on a panel of UCI-style datasets. Mukherjee et al. ( 2003 ) use learning-curve extrapolation to estimate sample-size requirements for DNA microarray classification. Figueroa et al. ( 2012 ) fit and invert learning curves to predict the sample size required to reach a target classification performance. Domhan et al. ( 2015 ) extrapolate learning curves to speed up hyperparameter optimization. The broader principle—treating error as a smooth, extrapolable function of a resource budget and using the resulting estimate to plan how much budget to spend—is shared with output-based error estimation in numerical analysis, where an adjoint-weighted error estimate directs where to add mesh resolution to reduce a target output’s error most efficiently (Ding et al. , 2016 ) ; the fitted a ​ N − b + c aN^{-b}+c plays the analogous role for labeled data, telling a practitioner how many additional rows buy a given error reduction. We do not claim novelty in the idea of fitting an a ​ N − b + c aN^{-b}+c law to classical models on tabular data. Our contribution is scale (127 replicators × \times 18 datasets × \times 6 model families), the protocol-level reproducibility lens (measuring spread across nominally compliant re-implementations), and the public release of aggregated curves and pooled fits as a benchmark resource. Tabular ML benchmarking. A parallel literature has shown repeatedly that on most tabular tasks, gradient boosting and random forests still beat deep architectures (Grinsztajn et al. , 2022 ; Shwartz-Ziv and Armon, 2022 ; Chen and Guestrin, 2016 ; Breiman, 2001 ) . The standard methodology in that literature, however, is to evaluate models at full data , not to trace error as a function of N N . Our work complements this by adding the sample-size axis: the ranking-at-full-data picture is enriched by knowing how quickly each family approaches its irreducible-error floor. Reproducibility and replication. Pineau et al. ( 2021 ) document the reproducibility crisis in machine learning and report on the NeurIPS Reproducibility Program. Bouthillier et al. ( 2019 ) argue that single-run reports systematically understate uncertainty: variance from seeds, data splits, and implementation details is real and large. Quantifying reliability is harder still when no gold-standard label is available: Ding ( 2025 ) address this with a variance-bounded evaluation framework that scores a system by its expected success across plausible interpretations, penalized by variance. Our replicator-spread estimate is a scaling-law analogue—it treats the variance of a reported exponent across nominally compliant re-implementations as a first-class quantity rather than a nuisance. Our 127-student design is, in effect, a controlled multi-replicator experiment whose primary product—in addition to the scaling laws themselves—is a quantitative estimate of how much a single research group’s reported scaling exponent should be trusted. 3 Methodology 3.1 Datasets We curated 18 publicly available tabular datasets covering business-relevant classification and regression tasks, summarized in Table 1 . Ten are classification (binary, with class imbalance ranging from 54%/46% to 88%/12%), and eight are regression. Sample sizes range from 303 ( heart_disease ) to 53,940 ( diamonds ). Feature counts range from 4 to 74, mixing numeric and categorical columns. All datasets are widely used in undergraduate and applied-ML courses, chosen because they admit straightforward preprocessing (one-hot encoding for categoricals, median imputation for the small number of missing values) and because the tasks are well-defined. Hyperparameters are fixed across all N N —no per- N N retuning—to keep results comparable across students and to isolate the data-size effect. For each (dataset, model) pair, students performed a single 80/20 train/test split with seed 42, then trained on nested subsets of the train fold at the seven fractions { 0.01 , 0.05 , 0.10 , 0.25 , 0.50 , 0.75 , 1.00 } \{0.01,\,0.05,\,0.10,\,0.25,\,0.50,\,0.75,\,1.00\} of the 80%-train pool. Subsets are nested (smaller subsets are subsets of larger ones) to reduce sampling noise across fractions. The same held-out 20% test set is used to evaluate every fraction. For classification we report 1 − AUROC 1-\mathrm{AUROC} as the error metric; for regression we report RMSE / std ​ ( y test ) \mathrm{RMSE}/\mathrm{std}(y_{\text{test}}) , i.e. RMSE normalized by the test-set standard deviation of the target. To bound SVM training time, classification SVMs were capped at a 10,000-row subsample of the training fraction. 3.3 Power-Law Fitting For each (student, dataset, model) triple we fit a three-parameter power law, error ​ ( N ) = a ​ N − b + c , a , b ≥ 0 , \mathrm{error}(N)\;=\;a\,N^{-b}\;+\;c,\qquad a,b\geq 0, (1) to the seven ( N , error ) (N,\mathrm{error}) points using non-linear least squares. Bounds on the irreducible-error floor are c ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] c\in[0,1] for classification (since 1 − AUROC ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] 1-\mathrm{AUROC}\in[0,1] ) and c ∈ [ 0 , 5 ] c\in[0,5] for regression. The exponent b b is bounded to [ 0 , 3 ] [0,3] . Fits with b b at the upper bound or with a a collapsing to zero are flagged but retained when reporting distributions. We use the threshold R 2 > 0.7 R^{2}>0.7 when reporting per-model exponent statistics (to exclude obviously failed fits without overpruning), and R 2 > 0.8 R^{2}>0.8 when counting “successful” fits in headline statements. 3.4 Classroom-Scale Aggregation The protocol of subsection 3.2 was executed independently by 127 students in a graduate ML course. Each student was assigned three datasets, spread across classification and regression. Per-(dataset, model) coverage ranges from 11 to 30 students depending on the random assignment (with SVM coverage slightly lower because a few students timed out on the largest classification datasets). In total this produced 11,536 individual model training runs and 1,648 student-level power-law fits that converged (per-student fit convergence: 100%; pooled-method failures: 0/80). We aggregate per-student fits to a population-level summary in two ways. The pooled approach concatenates all ( N , error ) (N,\mathrm{error}) points from all students for a given (dataset, model) and fits a single power law to the union; this is what we report for the data-requirement curves. The per-fraction-mean approach first averages error across students at each fraction and fits a power law to those seven means; we use this for robustness checks. Cross-student variance is reported as the coefficient of variation CV ​ ( b ) = σ b / μ b \mathrm{CV}(b)=\sigma_{b}/\mu_{b} of the fitted b b across students within a (dataset, model) cell that has at least 5 students. Because each student was assigned only 3 of 18 datasets, the per-cell CV ​ ( b ) \mathrm{CV}(b) is computed over a different subset of replicators for each (dataset, model) cell, so the design is partially blocked rather than fully crossed. We therefore treat the resulting variance as observational and the headline CV ​ ( b ) = 0.144 \mathrm{CV}(b)=0.144 as a marginal average over heterogeneous cells. 3.5 Cross-Dataset Combination To test whether a single exponent describes a model family across datasets, we combine per-cell evidence three ways. (i) Per-cell pooled fit : Equation 1 fit once per (dataset, model) on the union of student points. (ii) Shared-exponent joint fit : for each family we fit error d , i ​ ( N ) = a d ​ N − b model + c d \mathrm{error}_{d,i}(N)=a_{d}N^{-b_{\text{model}}}+c_{d} jointly across its datasets, sharing b model b_{\text{model}} while leaving ( a d , c d ) (a_{d},c_{d}) free per dataset ( scipy.optimize.least_squares with the bounds of subsection 3.3 ; soft- L 1 L_{1} loss for Lasso), compared to an unconstrained joint fit (free b d b_{d} ) by R 2 R^{2} and AIC on the same point cloud. (iii) Random-effects meta-analysis : within each cell with ≥ 5 \geq 5 students we pool b ^ \hat{b} via DerSimonian–Laird, using ( σ ^ b / n ) 2 (\hat{\sigma}_{b}/\sqrt{n})^{2} as within-study variance, and collapse per-student curves onto a normalised axis e norm = ( error − c ) / a e_{\text{norm}}=(\mathrm{error}-c)/a vs. N N . Upon acceptance we will release the aggregated ( N , error ) (N,\mathrm{error}) CSVs for all 11,536 runs, per-cell pooled fits, the data-requirement table, the analysis scripts, and the student-facing protocol skeleton at https://github.com/dingkaihua/classical_scaling . 4 Results 4.1 Power-Law Fits Across all 1,648 converged per-student fits, 77.7% achieve R 2 > 0.8 R^{2}>0.8 and 74.5% achieve R 2 > 0.9 R^{2}>0.9 , supporting the claim that the additive power law of Equation 1 is a useful description of how classical-ML test error scales with N N on tabular data. Fit quality is, however, very uneven across model families ( Table 2 ). Tree ensembles, SVM, and Linear/Logistic regression fit cleanly: 87.9–94.8% of their per-student fits exceed R 2 > 0.8 R^{2}>0.8 . Ridge and especially Lasso fit poorly, with only 47.5% and 23.8% respectively above that threshold. Table 2: R 2 R^{2} distribution per model family (all fits). Model mean median q25 q75 %fits R 2 > 0.8 R^{2}>0.8 Boosting 0.954 0.985 0.949 0.999 92.4% Lasso 0.546 0.649 0.443 0.703 23.8% LinearModel 0.910 0.967 0.916 0.997 90.4% RandomForest 0.947 0.971 0.956 0.991 87.9% Ridge 0.658 0.745 0.324 0.968 47.5% SVM 0.961 0.978 0.952 0.997 94.8% The poor Lasso and Ridge fits are mechanistic, not noise. Lasso shrinks all coefficients to zero in the small- N N regime under fixed regularization strength, producing a flat “predict-the-mean” error that is invariant to N N and incompatible with monotone power-law decay. Ridge shows a related pathology on california_housing , where the held-out RMSE briefly rises with N N at intermediate fractions before settling, which the power-law form ( Equation 1 ) cannot represent. We flag these mechanisms rather than discarding the cells: they are real findings about the limits of the power-law description for regularized linear models with fixed hyperparameters. The R 2 heatmap in Figure 4 makes the pattern visible at a glance. 4.2 Scaling Exponents and Irreducible Error The scaling exponent b b varies systematically across model families ( Figure 1 and Table 3 ). Random Forest has the smallest median exponent ( b ~ = 0.325 \tilde{b}=0.325 ): its error decays with N N but slowly, consistent with the high-variance averaging behavior of bagged trees. Boosting has a moderate exponent ( b ~ = 0.480 \tilde{b}=0.480 ). Linear/Logistic regression has the largest stable exponent ( b ~ = 0.830 \tilde{b}=0.830 ) on classification, reflecting the fact that low-capacity models gain more from each additional training point relative to their already-high error. Ridge has an even larger median exponent ( b ~ = 1.654 \tilde{b}=1.654 ) but with very wide spread and poor fit quality; we view it as a fitting artifact rather than a meaningful exponent. The median exponent across all good fits is 0.495 0.495 . Of classification fits, 47.7% have b > 0.5 b>0.5 and 76.5% have b > 0.3 b>0.3 . Of regression fits, 51.9% have b > 0.5 b>0.5 . Consistent with this, classification exponents are slightly higher than regression exponents within each family that does both: Boosting ( 0.575 0.575 clf vs. 0.508 0.508 reg), RandomForest ( 0.426 0.426 vs. 0.325 0.325 ), and SVM ( 1.023 1.023 vs. 0.745 0.745 ). The takeaway is that for practical decisions, b b alone is misleading; what matters is the joint ( b , c ) (b,c) . 4.3 Approximate Shared Exponents Across Datasets The per-dataset exponents of subsection 4.2 cluster strongly by model family. We test this directly: for each family we fit a single shared exponent b model b_{\text{model}} across all of its datasets while leaving the per-dataset level parameters ( a d , c d ) (a_{d},c_{d}) free ( subsection 3.5 ). Table 4 reports the comparison. Two facts must be read together. First, Δ ​ AIC ∈ [ + 65 , + 908 ] \Delta\mathrm{AIC}\in[+65,+908] strongly favors the unconstrained per-dataset fit on every family: the extra D − 1 D{-}1 free exponents capture residual structure that a single shared exponent cannot. Second, despite this, the pooled R 2 R^{2} gap is at most 0.011 0.011 for 5 of 6 families. We therefore read the result as approximate predictive compressibility rather than evidence for true equality of dataset-level exponents: a shared exponent loses very little explained variance on the pooled point cloud, while statistically real per-dataset heterogeneity in b b remains. (i) LODO transfer: refitting the shared- b b model on D − 1 D{-}1 datasets and predicting the held-out one gives median held-out R 2 R^{2} gaps of 0.007 0.007 – 0.035 0.035 for Boosting, RandomForest, LinearModel, and SVM, with b shared ( − d ) b_{\text{shared}}^{(-d)} stable across folds (CV 0.04 0.04 – 0.09 0.09 ); Ridge blows up (CV 0.96 0.96 ) and Lasso is meaningless. The headline 5-of-6 count refines under LODO to: strong held-out support for Boosting, RandomForest, LinearModel; moderate for SVM; fragile for Ridge; failure for Lasso (which we treat as a negative control). 4.4 Replicator-Implementation Variance The protocol fixes random_state=42 , so strictly compliant re-implementation should yield byte-identical fits. Of 71 (dataset, model) cells with ≥ 5 \geq 5 students, 13 (18%) have std ​ ( b ) < 10 − 10 \mathrm{std}(b)<10^{-10} , confirming the design floor. The remaining 58 cells show nonzero spread: unweighted mean CV ​ ( b ) = 0.144 \mathrm{CV}(b)=0.144 , size-weighted 0.131 0.131 , and 0.164 0.164 excluding the byte-identical cells (the upper bound on pure implementation noise). With the seed fixed this is not seed/sampling variance: it measures replicator-implementation spread induced by the unconstrained parts of the protocol (preprocessing, encoding, missing-value handling). SVM dominates (per-family weighted CV 0.25 0.25 ); the other families cluster in 0.08 0.08 – 0.20 0.20 . By regime: 36 cells (51%) at CV ​ ( b ) < 0.05 \mathrm{CV}(b)<0.05 (including the 13 byte-identical), 25 (35%) at 0.05 0.05 – 0.30 0.30 (legitimate protocol ambiguity), and 10 (14%) at ≥ 0.30 \geq 0.30 (more consistent with implementation bugs; e.g. RandomForest × \times diabetes_pima = 0.72 =0.72 ). Figure 2 shows this dispersion grows at small N N where preprocessing choices have the largest leverage. Thin lines: per-student curves; thick line: across-student mean; dashed line: pooled power-law fit. Per-student dispersion at small N N is visible; pooled fits are visibly tighter than any single student’s curve. The practical implication: single-group scaling-law studies should report uncertainty intervals on b b wide enough to accommodate this 14% floor; comparative claims (“model A has larger b b than B”) should require at minimum a ∼ 0.15 ​ b \sim 0.15\,b gap to be credible against protocol-drift noise. Pooling across students ( Figure 3 , dashed) gives tighter fits than any single student’s curve and underlies the data-requirement table below. 4.5 Data Requirements and Model Ranking From the pooled per-cell power-law fit, we invert Equation 1 to get the sample size N ⋆ N^{\star} required to reach a target error of 0.15 0.15 . Table 5 reports N ⋆ N^{\star} for each classification (dataset, model) cell where the target is reachable (i.e., where c < 0.15 c<0.15 ). On easy classification problems— adult_income , online_shoppers —tree ensembles get to 1 − AUROC = 0.15 1-\mathrm{AUROC}=0.15 with fewer than 400 training points. At the other extreme, telco_churn needs ∼ 16 , 500 \sim 16{,}500 points for Boosting to reach the target. Default-tuned tree ensembles dominate at full data, reproducing Grinsztajn et al. ( 2022 ) on a broader list and adding that they also have the most favorable ( b , c ) (b,c) profile. The data-requirement table gives concrete estimates: ∼ \sim 200–500 rows suffice to push 1 − AUROC < 0.15 1-\mathrm{AUROC}<0.15 on adult_income , bank_marketing , and online_shoppers with a booster, while telco_churn needs an order of magnitude more. Several cells have c c above the practical target—more data cannot help, and the right move is a better feature set, loss, or model class. For theory. Kaplan et al. ( 2020 ) report b ≈ 0.095 b\approx 0.095 for transformer loss and Hestness et al. ( 2017 ) b ≈ 0.07 b\approx 0.07 – 0.35 0.35 across modalities. Our classical exponents (median 0.495 0.495 ; 0.32 0.32 – 0.48 0.48 for tree ensembles; 0.83 0.83 for LinearModel on classification) are if anything larger than the small-NN exponents—each row buys more error reduction in classical tabular models than each token in a frontier transformer. What distinguishes the classical regime is the irreducible-error floor: tree ensembles routinely have c ≈ 0.10 c\approx 0.10 – 0.21 0.21 on classification, orders of magnitude larger than overparameterised LMs. In tabular ML the floor, not the exponent, is the binding constraint. Methodology. Treating a 127-student course as a population of independent replicators gives a near-free estimate of the protocol-drift floor on a scaling-law claim; the CV ​ ( b ) = 0.144 \mathrm{CV}(b)=0.144 figure is a concrete prior for single-group studies. Pooling across students ( Figure 3 ) also yields tighter fits than any individual curve at no extra compute cost. 6 Limitations (i) Fixed hyperparameters (no per- N N tuning), so our b b values are lower bounds for what proper model selection could achieve; Lasso/Ridge are most fragile under this constraint. (ii) Dataset coverage : 18 small-to-medium clean datasets (largest 53,940 rows); we say nothing about million-row settings. (iii) SVM cap : classification SVMs truncated to 10,000-row subsample, slightly suppressing large- N N behavior. (iv) Single split seed : with random_state=42 the CV ​ ( b ) = 0.144 \mathrm{CV}(b)=0.144 is replicator-implementation spread, not seed variance; a multi-seed study would report a larger total CV. (v) Imperfect replicators and partial blocking : each student saw only 3/18 datasets, so per-cell CV is computed over different sub-cohorts; cells with CV ​ ( b ) ≥ 0.30 \mathrm{CV}(b)\geq 0.30 (10/71) are more consistent with implementation bugs than legitimate ambiguity and we treat them as part of the phenomenon being measured. (vi) Shared-exponent stress tests are descriptive : supported in-sample (small gaps) and held-out (LODO for four families) but in-sample gap lacks specificity under permutation null and Ridge is fragile across folds ( Appendix A ). (vii) Agreement is not correctness : our shared-exponent evidence rests on independent per-student fits agreeing (low cross-student CV ​ ( b ) \mathrm{CV}(b) ), but agreement among independent estimators is necessary, not sufficient—shared implementation conventions can manufacture consensus—so low cross-student variance corroborates rather than proves a universal exponent (Ding, 2026 ) . 7 Conclusion A 127-student replication (18 datasets, 6 families) shows a ​ N − b + c aN^{-b}+c fits 77.7% of cells at R 2 > 0.8 R^{2}{>}0.8 ; a family-level exponent compresses cross-dataset curves for 5/6 families (Lasso fails); tree ensembles dominate at full data; fixed-seed CV ( b ) ≈ 0.14 (b)\!\approx\!0.14 .
